sense: of a seat, a bed, clothes, a journey

terms.grammar: adjective: with the dative or ad of what it suits
evidence: Liv. 22.2.2 (Lewis & Short): longius cēterum commodius iter
Ov. F. 2.288 (Lewis & Short): commoda vestis, of clothes for running
terms.comment: What fits its use well: a road, winter quarters, a garment for running. Of a person it means obliging, pleasant; commodum est is “it suits, it is convenient” (Lewis & Short). The opposite is incommodus, and the adverbs commodē, incommodē are “comfortably, uncomfortably”.
For a bed, a cushion or a seat, Latin says it is soft. Of people it is gentle, tender, and also weak or effeminate (Lewis & Short).
Traupman’s host’s phrase; suāviter is classical, “pleasantly”, but this use of it with esse was not found in Cicero’s letters, Plautus or Terence.

phrases.latin: Actiō māluimus iter facere pedibus quī incommodissimē nāvigāssēmus
phrases.english: from Actium we preferred to travel on foot, after a most uncomfortable voyage

phrases.latin: pr. Īdūs Oct. Athēnās vēnimus, cum sānē adversīs ventīs ūsī essēmus tardēque et incommodē nāvigāssēmus
phrases.english: we reached Athens on 14 October, after a voyage with contrary winds, slow and uncomfortable

phrases.latin: modo fac, id quod est hūmānitātis tuae, nē quid aliud cūrēs hōc tempore nisi ut quam commodissimē convalēscās
phrases.english: only see to it, as your good sense will, that for now you think of nothing but getting well as comfortably as you can
